design_detail: Two prospective community twin cohorts analysed in parallel, with a co-twin control analysis. RFAB (Risk Factors for Antisocial Behavior, Los Angeles): 614 families of twins and triplets (1,241 children) enrolled at 9–10 in 2001; WASI Vocabulary, Similarities, Block Design and Matrix Reasoning at 9–10 and again at 19–20. MTFS (Minnesota Twin Family Study): an original younger cohort (n=1,527, first assessed 1990–1996) and an Enrichment Study cohort (n=1,000, from 1999–2006) half of which was selected for disruptive behaviour and academic disengagement; WISC-R Vocabulary, Information, Block Design and Picture Arrangement at 11–12 and the WAIS-R versions at 17–19. Exposure: self-reported ever use of cannabis by follow-up; among people who used, 30 or more lifetime uses and daily use for 6 months or more. Mixed-effects models of change in age-standardized subtest scores (IQ metric), adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, SES and cohort, with supplementary adjustment for binge drinking and other drug use; co-twin comparisons within MZ and DZ pairs discordant for ever use (RFAB 25 MZ and 54 DZ pairs; MTFS 112 MZ and 99 DZ pairs) and within 47 MTFS pairs discordant for heavy use.
can_establish: Whether adolescents who went on to use cannabis by 17–20 fell further behind age peers on vocabulary and other Wechsler subtests than those who did not, in two US twin cohorts, and whether the twin who used differed from the co-twin who did not, a comparison that removes confounding shared by twins (all genes in MZ pairs, about half in DZ pairs, and the shared family environment).
cannot_establish: That cannabis has no effect on IQ, because the co-twin estimates are imprecise (the MZ intervals in both cohorts include the between-family difference), exposure is mostly ever use with few people who used heavily or for long, recency of use is unknown, follow-up ends at 17–20, and in RFAB many twins lacked exposure data or follow-up testing; nor can it show anything about full-scale IQ, executive function or memory, which were not tested.

sample.recruitment: Community twin samples: RFAB from greater Los Angeles school districts, socioeconomically and ethnically diverse (Hispanic 37%, Caucasian 27%, mixed 17%, African American 14%, Asian 5%; 52% female; 46% MZ); MTFS from two population-based Minnesota twin samples recruited at 11 and followed about every 3 years (51% female, 63% MZ, 93% Caucasian), the later one enriched for externalizing problems (Methods › Participants and Procedure).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Analytic samples: twins with a baseline IQ assessment and valid cannabis-use data, excluding those who reported use at baseline. RFAB 1,241, minus 24 without baseline IQ, 1 with use at baseline and 427 without cannabis data = 789; MTFS 2,527, minus 15, 15 and 220 = 2,277 (Table S1). For co-twin analyses the last-born of 14 triplet sets was excluded (RFAB 9, MTFS 5) (Methods › Statistical Analysis › Cotwin control).
sample.demographics: RFAB: age 9.6 at baseline in both groups and 19.5 (never used) against 20.0 (used) at follow-up; 43.9% against 46.7% male; MZ 51.1% against 40.7%. MTFS: 11.8 at baseline; 18.0 against 18.2 at follow-up; 44.6% against 55.0% male; SES percentile 52.1 against 48.6; Caucasian 95.3% against 88.9%. The cannabis group had far more other drug use (RFAB 38.3% against 1.6%; MTFS 39.4% against 6.6%) and heavier maximal drinking (Table 1).
sample.attrition: RFAB: 427 of 1,216 eligible twins (35%) lacked cannabis-use data and were excluded; of the 789 analysed, 323 did not complete follow-up IQ testing (466 tested), and their baseline scores were kept in maximum-likelihood models assuming data missing at random; follow-up n per subtest 438–459. MTFS: 220 of 2,497 (9%) excluded for missing cannabis data; follow-up attrition 10–20%; Information and Picture Arrangement were not given to the Enrichment sample at follow-up (follow-up n 1,252 and 1,000) (Results › Description of Analytic Sample, 2nd paragraph; Tables S1–S3). The eligible totals, percentages and per-subtest follow-up totals are editors' arithmetic from Tables S1–S3.
sample.selection_effects: Twins without cannabis data had lower SES and baseline IQ in both cohorts and in RFAB were more often male, MZ and non-white (Table S2); the authors expect people with heavier use to be under-represented at later waves, biasing towards the null (Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph). Half of the MTFS Enrichment sample was selected for disruptive behaviour and academic disengagement, which enriches MTFS for the confounders at issue; the two MTFS samples were combined with cohort as a covariate.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at each wave, without biological verification. RFAB: a survey question on ever trying cannabis at each wave, and at wave 5 questions on daily use for at least 6 months and on 30 or more lifetime uses, completed in the laboratory or at home by mail or online. MTFS: structured interviews (DICA at 11 and 14; CIDI Substance Abuse Module at 17) and a computerized survey completed in private at 14 and 17 (and 11 for the Enrichment sample); ever use taken as the highest endorsement across instruments; agreement between survey and interview for ever use κ = 0.86 at 14 and 0.91 at 17, with 46 of 238 who reported use in the private survey (19%) denying it at interview (Methods › Assessment of marijuana use; Measurement of Marijuana Use in the Minnesota Twin Family Study, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Ever use on any occasion against never. Among people who used: 30 or more lifetime uses (RFAB 49.3%, MTFS 37.0%) and daily use for 6 months or more (20.8% and 22.6%) (Table 1). Recency, current against former use, route and potency were not measured; in MTFS the heaviest period of daily use most often began at 16 (Measurement of Marijuana Use in the Minnesota Twin Family Study, 5th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drug use (yes/no across 10 drug classes, plus nitrous oxide in RFAB) and maximal binge drinking (largest number of drinks in a day, log-transformed and winsorized) were measured. Primary models did not adjust for them, to maximize the chance of detecting an association with cannabis; supplementary models did (Tables S4 and S5). Binge-drinking data cover 270 and 421 RFAB twins (Table 1 footnote).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not measured; the authors state they could not separate current from former heavy use or acute from non-acute effects (Discussion › Limitations, 4th paragraph).

comparison.controls: Twins who reported never using cannabis by follow-up (RFAB 314; MTFS 1,455); in the co-twin analyses, the co-twin who never used.
comparison.matching: Co-twin control matches on everything twins share (all genes in MZ pairs, about half in DZ pairs; family environment); DZ models adjust for sex. Between-family models adjust for age, sex, race, zygosity, SES (RFAB: Hollingshead index percentile at baseline; MTFS: composite of income, both parents' education and parental occupation) and MTFS cohort.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline subtests were measured before use. Not adjusted: childhood conduct problems, attention problems and delinquency, parental monitoring and the other family-culture factors the authors propose as the confounders (Discussion › Are Developmentally Emerging IQ Deficits Found in Those Who Use Marijuana Widespread or Specific?, 2nd paragraph). Within pairs, factors that differ between co-twins (peers, individual behaviour problems) remain uncontrolled.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Other drug use was reported by 1.6% (RFAB) and 6.6% (MTFS) of the never-used group (Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: RFAB: WASI Vocabulary, Similarities, Block Design and Matrix Reasoning (the same test at both ages). MTFS: WISC-R Vocabulary, Information, Block Design and Picture Arrangement at 11–12, then the WAIS-R versions at 17–19 (Enrichment sample: Vocabulary and Block Design only). Scaled scores were age-standardized and converted to an IQ metric (mean 100, SD 15). WAIS-III Digit Span was given at 17–18 to 1,452 MTFS twins, at follow-up only (Methods › Assessment of intelligence; Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard Wechsler norms. WISC-R and WAIS-R items differ, so only change in age-standardized scores, not raw scores, can be compared (Methods › Assessment of intelligence, 3rd paragraph). No full-scale IQ was computed.
outcomes.operationalization: Decline = a more negative change in the age-standardized score of the cannabis group than of the never-used group (time-by-group interaction), that is, falling behind age peers; in co-twin analyses, the within-pair difference in change. Vocabulary and Information are classed as crystallized ability, Block Design, Matrix Reasoning and Picture Arrangement as fluid ability, and Similarities as both.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 6 subtests (4 per cohort; Vocabulary and Block Design in both) are each tested in the main models (8 cohort-subtest tests), the frequency models among people who used (16), the co-twin models by zygosity (16), the substance-adjusted supplementary models (24) and the heavy-use co-twin models (4): about 68 tests at P < 0.05 (editors' count).

analysis.effect_sizes: Difference in change, cannabis group minus never-used group, in IQ points (time-by-group interaction), adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, SES and cohort (Table 3): Vocabulary RFAB −4.0 (95% CI −6.3 to −1.7), P = 0.001, and MTFS −3.4 (−4.5 to −2.3), P < 0.001; Information (MTFS) −2.0 (−3.3 to −0.7), P = 0.002; Similarities (RFAB) −0.1 (−2.8 to 2.5); Block Design RFAB 0.2 (−2.0 to 2.5) and MTFS −0.6 (−1.8 to 0.6); Matrix Reasoning (RFAB) 1.9 (−0.7 to 4.4); Picture Arrangement (MTFS) 0.4 (−1.6 to 2.4). With binge drinking and other drug use added (Table S4): Vocabulary RFAB −3.7 (−6.8 to −0.5), P = 0.022, and MTFS −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6), P = 0.244; Information −0.7 (−2.3 to 0.9), P = 0.399. Vocabulary per year of age: RFAB +0.01 (never used) and −0.39 (used), difference 0.397 per year, about 4 points over 10 years; MTFS +0.12 and −0.45, difference 0.57, about 4 points over 7 years; difference between cohorts 0.176, P = 0.35. Within people who used (Table 4), Vocabulary: 30 or more uses RFAB −0.8 (−4.2 to 2.6) and MTFS −0.6 (−2.4 to 1.2); daily use RFAB −0.4 (−4.5 to 3.7) and MTFS −0.7 (−2.7 to 1.4); no subtest significant, also after substance adjustment (Table S5). Co-twin (Table 5), Vocabulary: RFAB MZ −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5, 25 pairs) and DZ −2.8 (−7.7 to 2.2, 54 pairs); MTFS MZ −0.7 (−3.9 to 2.4, 112 pairs) and DZ 0.2 (−2.8 to 3.3, 99 pairs); the only significant co-twin result was Matrix Reasoning in RFAB DZ pairs, 6.6 (0.6 to 12.7), P = 0.036, in favour of the twin who used. Pairs discordant for heavy use (MTFS, 47; Table S6): Vocabulary −1.5 (−5.5 to 2.6), Information 0.2 (−5.1 to 5.6), Block Design −1.6 (−7.3 to 4.1), Picture Arrangement 5.2 (−4.1 to 14.6).
analysis.covariates: Age, sex, race, zygosity, SES and MTFS cohort in the main models; maximal binge drinking and other drug use added in the supplementary models; sex in the DZ co-twin models.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan reported; three criteria for a causal effect (use precedes decline, dose-response, persistence after adjusting for genes and upbringing) are stated in the introduction (5th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Every subtest is reported, including non-significant results, and the supplementary analyses are shown (Tables S1–S6). Not shown: the co-twin estimates pooled across MZ and DZ pairs, which the text says were not significant (Results › Cotwin Control Analyses, 1st paragraph); and several printed co-twin P values do not match their intervals (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: No power analysis. The authors argue the larger MTFS gave the same conclusion (Discussion › Can Within-Pair Differences in IQ Be Attributed to a Possible Causal Effect of Marijuana Use?, 2nd paragraph); but the MZ co-twin intervals for Vocabulary (RFAB −11.2 to 0.5; MTFS −3.9 to 2.4) include the between-family differences of −4.0 and −3.4, so the co-twin analyses cannot tell no within-pair effect from one as large as the between-family association (editors' reading of Tables 3 and 5).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In both cohorts, twins who had used cannabis by 17–20 changed 3.4 to 4.0 points less on Vocabulary than twins who had not (a difference in change: on the raw means those who used fell 1.8 and 2.5 points while those who did not rose 1.8 and 1.3) (and 2.0 points on Information in MTFS), with no difference on Similarities, Block Design, Matrix Reasoning or Picture Arrangement. In MTFS, future cannabis use already went with lower Vocabulary, Information and Block Design scores at 11–12, and the Vocabulary and Information differences in change shrank to non-significance after adjustment for drinking and other drug use (−0.8 and −0.7); in RFAB the Vocabulary difference did not (−3.7). Among people who used, 30 or more uses or daily use did not go with more change. Within discordant twin pairs no Vocabulary difference was significant; the RFAB MZ estimate was −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5, 25 pairs) and the MTFS MZ estimate −0.7 (−3.9 to 2.4, 112 pairs).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the observed declines may not be a direct result of cannabis but attributable to familial factors, the significance statement that familial confounds underlie the association, and the conclusion that the deficits are attributable to confounding factors rather than a neurotoxic effect. Gaps: (1) non-significant within-pair differences are read as the absence of an effect, although the MZ intervals in both cohorts include the between-family association and the RFAB MZ point estimate (−5.4) is larger than the between-family estimate (−4.0), while the interval for the 99 MTFS DZ pairs (−2.8 to 3.3) excludes the between-family −3.4; (2) the conclusion counts baseline differences before use among its three grounds, but these were found only in MTFS, not in RFAB; (3) the discussion says the Vocabulary association was completely eliminated in MTFS after adjustment for other substances (Discussion › Are the Deficits in Crystallized Intelligence Specific to Marijuana Use?, 1st paragraph), while the estimate fell to −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6), and drinking and other drug use may lie on a common pathway rather than only confound; (4) the absence of a dose-response rests on two binary contrasts among people who mostly used lightly, with RFAB intervals of about ±4 points; (5) the conclusion about intellectual decline in general rests on 6 subtests over adolescence, with no full-scale IQ, memory or executive measure; (6) the inference that family environment rather than genes is the source, because DZ estimates were not larger than MZ estimates (Discussion › Can Within-Pair Differences…, 1st paragraph), compares imprecise estimates without a test. The authors' limitations section concedes that effects of long-term or recent use cannot be ruled out.

timeline.event: Lyons et al. (Psychological Medicine): adult twins discordant for regular cannabis use differed little on tests, with one Block Design difference that its authors attributed to type 1 error; cited by Jackson et al. as concordant (Discussion › Can Within-Pair Differences…, 2nd paragraph).

Fried, Watkinson & Gray (Neurotoxicology and Teratology): IQ declines in people currently using cannabis heavily but not in people who formerly used heavily, as cited in the introduction (3rd paragraph).
Meier et al. (Dunedin): IQ decline with persistent cannabis dependence, the study this paper sets out to test (card sc_meier_2012).

Rogeberg (PNAS): SES confounding as an explanation of the Dunedin result; Jackson et al. report no attenuation after adjusting for their SES composite (card sc_rogeberg_2013). The original authors' SES reanalysis (Moffitt et al., 2013; card sc_moffitt_2013) is not cited.

This study: two twin cohorts with parallel analyses; the Vocabulary association with ever use and the null co-twin estimates appear in both, while baseline differences and attenuation by other substance use appear only in MTFS.

Meier et al. (Addiction), a longitudinal co-twin control study of adolescent cannabis use and neuropsychological decline, in the project's Tier A list and carded in this round by another reader; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: Within this paper the two cohorts agree on a between-family association of ever use with vocabulary decline of about 3.4 to 4.0 points over adolescence and on non-significant co-twin differences, and disagree on baseline differences and on attenuation by other substance use. The co-twin estimates are the most-cited result but are imprecise, and the exposure (mostly ever use by 17–20) is far lighter and shorter than the persistent dependence to 38 studied in Dunedin (Meier et al., 2012), so the two studies do not test the same contrast. Later co-twin studies in the project's lists (Meier et al., 2018; Schaefer et al., 2022) are needed for a claim about where the question stands; they are not read here.

funding.funder: National Institute of Mental Health Grant R01-MH58354 (RFAB) and NIH Grants DA 013240, DA 05147, DA036216 and AA 09367 (MTFS) (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: "The authors declare no conflict of interest." (Footnotes). PNAS Direct Submission; edited by Valerie F. Reyna (Cornell University), a guest editor invited by the Editorial Board; received 20 August 2015, accepted 14 December 2015 (author information).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at the University of Southern California (RFAB), the University of Minnesota (MTFS), UCLA, Örebro University and the University of Pennsylvania; W.G.I., M.M., A.R. and L.A.B. designed the research, and N.J.J. and J.D.I. (equal contribution) analysed the data and wrote the paper.

what_would_settle_it: Co-twin or sibling studies with enough pairs discordant for heavy, persistent use (not ever use) followed into adulthood, with repeated full-scale IQ and memory and executive testing, biologically verified exposure and recency, and an equivalence margin stated in advance, so that a null within-pair estimate could be read as evidence of no effect rather than as an imprecise result.

domains.note: Judged for the co-twin estimates, which carry the paper's conclusion: they remove confounding shared by twins, but not factors that differ between co-twins (peers, individual conduct problems). The between-family estimates in Table 3 would be at high risk, as the paper's own baseline differences and attenuation by other substance use show.

Self-reported ever use, verified only by agreement between instruments in MTFS (κ 0.86–0.91); frequency as two binary measures; recency unknown; any misclassification of the never-using co-twin biases the co-twin estimates towards the null.
Community twin samples, but half of the MTFS Enrichment sample was selected for externalizing problems, and twins without cannabis data, who had lower SES and IQ, were excluded (see missing data).

RFAB: 35% of eligible twins excluded for missing cannabis data and 41% of the analysed twins without follow-up IQ, handled by maximum likelihood assuming data missing at random, although missingness went with lower SES and IQ and, the authors expect, heavier use. MTFS: 9% excluded and 10–20% attrition, with two subtests not given to the Enrichment sample at follow-up (some concerns on its own).
Standardized Wechsler subtests, but no full-scale IQ, different item pools across WISC-R and WAIS-R in MTFS and a short form for the Enrichment sample; testers' blinding not reported.
About 68 tests without correction; pooled MZ and DZ co-twin estimates not shown; several printed P values do not match their intervals; but all subtests and supplementary models are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain, here missing data in RFAB. The co-twin design is a real strength against confounding by family and genes, and the use of two cohorts adds a built-in replication. But the co-twin estimates are too imprecise to show the absence of an effect, exposure is mostly ever use within a few years of adolescence, and in RFAB missing data are large and related to SES and IQ. Citable for the between-family association of ever use with vocabulary and information decline, the MTFS baseline differences, the attenuation after adjustment for other substance use in MTFS, and the co-twin estimates with their intervals; not as evidence that cannabis does not affect IQ, nor for heavy, long-term or recent use.

key_findings.finding: Analytic samples: RFAB 789 twins from 436 families and MTFS 2,277 twins from 1,171 families; 427 RFAB and 220 MTFS twins were excluded for missing cannabis-use data, and these twins had lower SES and baseline IQ (for example RFAB Vocabulary 96.5 against 101.9; MTFS 97.6 against 100.2).
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of Analytic Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Tables S1 and S2

key_findings.finding: In RFAB, 323 of the 789 analysed twins did not complete follow-up IQ testing (466 tested); their baseline data were kept in maximum-likelihood models. MTFS follow-up attrition was 10–20%, and Information and Picture Arrangement were not given to the Enrichment sample at follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of Analytic Sample, 2nd paragraph; Table S3

key_findings.finding: 60% of RFAB twins (475 of 789) and 36% of MTFS twins (822 of 2,277), who were about 2 years younger at follow-up, had used cannabis; among them 49.3% and 37.0% had used it 30 or more times and 20.8% and 22.6% daily for 6 months or more.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of Analytic Sample, 3rd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Baseline scores, before any cannabis use: no differences in RFAB at 9–10; in MTFS at 11–12, future cannabis use went with lower Vocabulary (−1.9, P < 0.01), Information (−2.7, P < 0.001) and Block Design (−2.0, P < 0.01); no baseline differences in Similarities, Matrix Reasoning or Picture Arrangement.
key_findings.locator: Results › Baseline Differences in IQ, 1st paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Table 2's MTFS Information means (97.9 against 101.2) give a raw difference of −3.3, not the −2.7 in the text; the other two differences match the table.

key_findings.finding: Difference in change, cannabis group minus never-used group, adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, SES and cohort: Vocabulary −4.0 points (95% CI −6.3 to −1.7) in RFAB and −3.4 (−4.5 to −2.3) in MTFS; Information −2.0 (−3.3 to −0.7) in MTFS; Block Design, Similarities, Matrix Reasoning and Picture Arrangement not different (estimates −0.6 to 1.9, all intervals including 0).
key_findings.locator: Results › IQ Change Between Marijuana User Groups, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3; Fig. 1
key_findings.note: A difference in change between groups: on the Table 2 means, Vocabulary in those who used fell 1.8 points (RFAB, 99.9 to 98.1) and 2.5 points (MTFS, 98.8 to 96.3), while in those who never used it rose 1.8 (100.2 to 102.0) and 1.3 (100.7 to 102.0), so about half of each gap is the comparison group's rise (editors' arithmetic). Fig. 1, named in the locator, was not inspected by the second reader or the adjudicator.

key_findings.finding: With maximal binge drinking and other drug use added, the Vocabulary difference was −3.7 (−6.8 to −0.5, P = 0.022) in RFAB but −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6, P = 0.244) in MTFS, and the MTFS Information difference −0.7 (−2.3 to 0.9); the authors suggest drinking may predict IQ decline less in the college-age RFAB sample.
key_findings.locator: Results › IQ Change Between Marijuana User Groups, 1st paragraph; Table S4; Discussion › Are the Deficits in Crystallized Intelligence Specific to Marijuana Use?, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Among people who used cannabis, 30 or more uses and daily use for 6 months or more were not associated with more change on any subtest (Vocabulary, 30 or more uses: RFAB −0.8, −4.2 to 2.6; MTFS −0.6, −2.4 to 1.2; daily use: RFAB −0.4, −4.5 to 3.7; MTFS −0.7, −2.7 to 1.4), also after substance adjustment.
key_findings.locator: Results › IQ Change Between Marijuana User Groups, 3rd paragraph; Tables 4 and S5
key_findings.note: The authors say their data do not allow a full examination of dose-dependent effects.

key_findings.finding: Vocabulary change per year of age: RFAB (n=785) +0.01 in the never-used group (P = 0.90) and −0.39 in the cannabis group (P < 0.001), a difference of 0.397 a year, or about a 4-point gap over 10 years; MTFS (n=2,271) +0.12 (P = 0.028) and −0.45 (P < 0.001), a difference of 0.57 a year, or 4.0 points over 7 years; the two cohorts did not differ (Δ0.176, P = 0.35).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of Effect Size Between RFAB and MTFS, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Co-twin comparisons of twins discordant for ever use showed no significant difference in change for Vocabulary (RFAB MZ −5.4, −11.2 to 0.5, 25 pairs; DZ −2.8, −7.7 to 2.2, 54 pairs; MTFS MZ −0.7, −3.9 to 2.4, 112 pairs; DZ 0.2, −2.8 to 3.3, 99 pairs), Similarities, Information, Block Design or Picture Arrangement; in RFAB DZ pairs the twin who used gained more on Matrix Reasoning (6.6, 0.6 to 12.7, P = 0.036). Pooling MZ and DZ pairs is said to leave all estimates non-significant (not shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cotwin Control Analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 5
key_findings.note: The MZ intervals include the between-family Vocabulary differences (−4.0 RFAB, −3.4 MTFS), so these results are compatible with both no within-pair effect and an effect of that size. In the largest discordant group, the 99 MTFS non-identical pairs, the interval (−2.8 to 3.3) excludes the between-family difference of −3.4, so in that cohort the co-twin evidence leans towards a smaller within-pair effect.

key_findings.finding: In 47 MTFS pairs in which one twin never used and the other used frequently (more than 30 uses or a period of daily use), no subtest differed: Vocabulary −1.5 (−5.5 to 2.6), Information 0.2 (−5.1 to 5.6), Block Design −1.6 (−7.3 to 4.1), Picture Arrangement 5.2 (−4.1 to 14.6).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cotwin Control Analyses, 2nd paragraph; Table S6

key_findings.finding: Digit Span (WAIS-III), given at 17–18 to 1,452 MTFS twins: mean 9.4 (SD 2.4) in the cannabis group against 9.2 (SD 2.4) in the never-used group; follow-up only, with no test reported.

The authors interpret the absence of larger effects in DZ than in MZ pairs as pointing to family-wide environment rather than genes, and propose family-cultural factors (less parental monitoring, less emphasis on scholarship) rather than material SES as the confounders, noting that the deficits are specific to measures of acquired knowledge.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Can Within-Pair Differences in IQ Be Attributed to a Possible Causal Effect of Marijuana Use?, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Are Developmentally Emerging IQ Deficits Found in Those Who Use Marijuana Widespread or Specific?, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: exposure was mostly measured as discrete categories without recency; participants were young adults at the last assessment, so effects of more prolonged use could not be ruled out, which they offer as a possible reason for the difference from Meier et al. (2012), whose participants were 38; current and former heavy use could not be separated; and attrition may have removed people who used more heavily.

reporting_issues.issue: Several co-twin P values in Table 5 do not match their confidence intervals: RFAB Matrix Reasoning MZ 5.7 (−1.5 to 13.0) is printed P = 0.305, but the interval implies about 0.12; MTFS Information DZ −2.5 (−6.9 to 1.9) is printed P = 0.545, implying about 0.27; RFAB Vocabulary MZ −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5) is printed P = 0.098, implying about 0.07 (editors' calculation, normal approximation from the interval).
reporting_issues.consequence: No result changes significance, but the RFAB MZ Vocabulary estimate, the one that runs in the causal direction and exceeds the between-family estimate, is closer to significance than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the MTFS baseline Information difference as −2.7, while Table 2's means (97.9 against 101.2) give −3.3; the Vocabulary and Block Design differences in the text match the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the text reports a model-based estimate without saying so or one value is wrong; claims should cite the table means with the text's test.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says the Vocabulary association was completely eliminated in MTFS after adjustment for other substance use, but Table S4 gives −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6).
reporting_issues.consequence: The association was attenuated by about three quarters and became non-significant; it was not eliminated.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion lists baseline differences before cannabis use as one of three grounds for attributing the association to confounding, but such differences were found only in MTFS; in RFAB there were none at 9–10 (Results › Baseline Differences in IQ, 1st paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: The argument that lower scores precede cannabis use rests on one of the two cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says Meier et al. (2012) found no significant differences on visuospatial tests such as Block Design and Picture Arrangement; Meier et al. tested Picture Completion, not Picture Arrangement (Meier et al., 2012, Table 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error; the comparison of specific subtests across the two studies should be made from the primary tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The Vocabulary means plotted in Fig. 1 differ from the Table 2 means (for example, the RFAB never-used group starts at about 99.4 in the figure and 100.2 in the table), and the legend does not say whether the figure shows model estimates; the year-of-age analysis uses 785 and 2,271 twins against analytic samples of 789 and 2,277, without explanation.

disagreements.first_pass: In both cohorts, twins who had used cannabis by 17–20 fell 3.4 to 4.0 points further behind age peers on Vocabulary than twins who had not (and 2.0 points on Information in MTFS), with no difference on Similarities, Block Design, Matrix Reasoning or Picture Arrangement. In MTFS, future cannabis use already went with lower Vocabulary, Information and Block Design scores at 11–12, and the Vocabulary and Information differences in change shrank to non-significance after adjustment for drinking and other drug use (−0.8 and −0.7); in RFAB the Vocabulary difference did not (−3.7). Among people who used, 30 or more uses or daily use did not go with more change. Within discordant twin pairs no Vocabulary difference was significant; the RFAB MZ estimate was −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5, 25 pairs) and the MTFS MZ estimate −0.7 (−3.9 to 2.4, 112 pairs). | The abstract says the observed declines may not be a direct result of cannabis but attributable to familial factors, the significance statement that familial confounds underlie the association, and the conclusion that the deficits are attributable to confounding factors rather than a neurotoxic effect. Gaps: (1) non-significant within-pair differences are read as the absence of an effect, although the MZ intervals in both cohorts include the between-family association and the RFAB MZ point estimate (−5.4) is larger than the between-family estimate (−4.0); (2) the conclusion counts baseline differences before use among its three grounds, but these were found only in MTFS, not in RFAB; (3) the discussion says the Vocabulary association was completely eliminated in MTFS after adjustment for other substances (Discussion › Are the Deficits in Crystallized Intelligence Specific to Marijuana Use?, 1st paragraph), while the estimate fell to −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6), and drinking and other drug use may lie on a common pathway rather than only confound; (4) the absence of a dose-response rests on two binary contrasts among people who mostly used lightly, with RFAB intervals of about ±4 points; (5) the conclusion about intellectual decline in general rests on 6 subtests over adolescence, with no full-scale IQ, memory or executive measure; (6) the inference that family environment rather than genes is the source, because DZ estimates were not larger than MZ estimates (Discussion › Can Within-Pair Differences…, 1st paragraph), compares imprecise estimates without a test. The authors' limitations section concedes that effects of long-term or recent use cannot be ruled out.

disagreements.resolution: Accepted; wording and balance corrected. Gap rating unchanged (substantial; reader 214 agrees).
